newsitem.title: UK: Dollar surge favours European bonds now, U.S. later.
newsitem.headline: Dollar surge favours European bonds now, U.S. later.

text.p: A dollar surge has underpinned some European bond markets but after a pair of important policy meetings in the coming days, U.S. Treasuries are likely to look more attractive to investors, analysts said on Thursday.
The U.S. Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the Federal Reserve's policy arm, is to meet on February 4-5. The Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations then gathers on February 8.
"Initially on a dollar rally, Europe outperforms the U.S.," said Michael O'Hanlon, chief international economist at PaineWebber in London.
Although it appears contrary, dollar strength actually helps European markets by curbing the mark and fostering yield convergence against Bunds, analysts said.

"When the dollar starts to stabilise, the U.S. market then looks cheap," said O'Hanlon. "At the same time you start to see stronger export growth coming through in Europe which tends to undermine the performance you have just seen in European bond markets."

Going into the two meetings, few expect dramatic developments for the market. The FOMC is widely expected to keep interest rates unchanged and the G7 is likely to shy away from any concrete decisions to push back the dollar, analysts said.
"We should brush over the FOMC this time," said O'Hanlon, "The market always pays attention to any FOMC meeting, but if we don't get any move it will be no surprise."

Dick Howard, director of economic research at Julius Baer Investments in London, said the reality of G7 meetings was usually less riveting than the buildup. "For some time G7 meetings have been more threatening to currency markets in the expectation than in the outcome," he said.
U.S. Treasuries were starting to look like good value relative to German debt, analysts said.
O'Hanlon said that in the past, as the U.S./German 10-year yield spread neared the 100 basis point level, this had signalled a buying opportunity for the U.S..

"We are close to that now," he said. "I suspect we won't actually break the 100 level this time round but the main data to focus on is next Friday's payrolls. If the data are soft enough relative to expectations, that spread is likely to reverse and go back towards 50."
The T-note/Bund spread is currently at 94 basis points, having stretched out from 50 basis points in early December.

Analysts said dollar stabilisation would ensue as moderating export trends slowed the economy. "Roughly 40 to 45 percent of S&P 500 earnings are generated overseas, and of that about a quarter is generated in Europe," said O'Hanlon.

"So, whenever we see the dollar rallying it risks slowing export growth and that is an important consideration for multinational U.S. companies," he said. "That should mean that once the dollar stabilises, the U.S. bond market will potentially look cheap at high yield levels."

Howard said from a domestic point of view, a strong currency was usually good for bond markets because it tightened monetary conditions and helped to dampen inflation expectations, but this so far had not been the case for U.S. Treasuries.
"The relationship between currencies and bond markets is never straightforward," he said. "It depends on whether interest rates are leading the currency or if the currency is leading interest rates."
But the current situation in the U.S. is that interest rate expectations are leading the dollar, Howard said. "That is what has unsettled the bond market," he said.
But Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist Europe at BankAmerica in London, said that while the dollar was a factor for Treasuries, domestic matters were far more of a concern.

The outlook for Treasuries would improve if interest rates were not raised at next week's FOMC meeting and key U.S. data, including GDP on Friday and the unemployment report next week, came in on the soft side.
"Then there will be scope to see Treasuries bouncing back a bit," he said.
